question: A regular polygon of \(n\) sides is inscribed in a circle of radius \(R.\) The area of the polygon is \(3R^2.\) Then \(n\) equals:
solution:
Joining the circle’s center to every vertex divides the polygon into \(n\) congruent triangles. Each has two sides of length \(R>0\) and included angle \(360^\circ/n\). Dropping an altitude gives its area as \(\tfrac12R^2\sin(360^\circ/n)\). Thus the polygon’s area is
\[
A_n=\frac n2R^2\sin\frac{360^\circ}{n}.
\]
For \(n=12\), the central angle is \(30^\circ\), and therefore
\[
A_{12}=6R^2\sin30^\circ=3R^2.
\]
We also need to know that another number of sides cannot give the same area. Here is an elementary comparison that avoids calculus. Take integers \(3\le p<q\), and put \(\delta=360^\circ/(pq)\). The sine addition formulas give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sin(k\delta)-\sin((k-1)\delta)\\
&\qquad=2\sin\frac\delta2\cos\left(k-\frac12\right)\delta.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(1\le k\le q\), these cosine angles increase from a positive angle to less than \(360^\circ/p\le120^\circ\). Cosine strictly decreases on this range, as its unit-circle horizontal coordinate moves left. Hence the displayed successive sine differences strictly decrease.

The average of their first \(p\) terms is therefore greater than the average of their first \(q\) terms. Their sums telescope, giving
\[
\frac{\sin(p\delta)}p>\frac{\sin(q\delta)}q.
\]
Multiplication by \(pq\) yields
\[
q\sin\frac{360^\circ}{q}
>
p\sin\frac{360^\circ}{p},
\]
so \(A_q>A_p\). The polygon area strictly increases with the integer number of sides. Consequently \(n=12\) is the unique answer, choice C.

edges.reason: Interior angle sums help with angle work. However, radius and apothem come from the central angle 360/n and a right triangle, and the interior angle follows from the central angle too.
The triangle circumcircle introduces circles through all vertices, which eases the generalization. Regular polygon center and radius can be defined via symmetry or equal division of a circle.
edges.scope: circumscribed circle of a regular polygon

edges.reason: Angle-independent ratios use proportional sides of similar right triangles.
A special trigonometric value is a value of the corresponding side ratio.
Right-triangle ratios motivate the unit-circle definition and help compute sin 30°. The coordinate definition stands alone and covers non-acute angles that ratios cannot.
edges.scope: motivating unit-circle definitions from right-triangle ratios

edges.reason: One explicit criterion is to distinguish the signs of sum and difference formulas. That comparison requires the relevant difference formulas, even though a direct derivation of the sum formula alone could avoid them.
edges.scope: Distinguishing the signs in the sine/cosine sum and difference formulas

edges.reason: Triangle classification helps recognize where an altitude may lie. The area relation and a supplied base/height can be used across all triangle types without first sorting them as acute, right or obtuse.
edges.scope: locating heights in right and obtuse triangles

edges.reason: The target explicitly states that the triangle has half the area of an equal-base equal-height parallelogram. Parallelogram-area meaning is needed for that specified comparison.
